library.title: Markets trade the surprise, not the level
library.text: Investors already expect a number (the consensus). Prices move on the gap between the actual and that expectation.

library.title: Two channels: cash flows and the discount rate
library.text: Every headline reaches prices through expected profits, the discount rate, or both. A strong jobs report can lift profits and yields at the same time: the net effect decides.

library.title: Good news can be bad news
library.text: When inflation is the main worry, strong data raises the odds of higher rates, and stocks can fall on it.

library.title: In a cap-weighted index, the giants decide
library.text: A handful of mega-caps make up a large share of the S&P 500. The index can fall on a day when most of its stocks rise, and the reverse.

library.title: The Dow is price-weighted
library.text: The Dow weights companies by share price, not size. A few high-priced stocks can push it the other way from the S&P 500.

library.title: Growth stocks behave like long bonds
library.text: Most of a growth company's value sits in profits far in the future. When rates or confidence change, those distant cash flows swing the most.

library.title: One company's revenue is another's cost
library.text: The AI build-out helps the sellers of chips and memory and squeezes the buyers. 'Tech' is not one block.

library.title: Markets hate uncertainty more than bad news
library.text: Fear spikes when the outcome is unknown; once it is known, volatility often fades even if the news is bad.

library.title: Flight to quality
library.text: In a scare, money leaves risky assets for safe ones: Treasuries rally (yields fall), and the dollar, yen, Swiss franc and gold tend to firm.

library.title: Supply shocks are the hardest case
library.text: An oil shock pushes inflation up and growth down at the same time, leaving central banks with no good option.

library.title: Look at real rates
library.text: Policy is only tight if the rate is well above inflation. Rate minus inflation tells you how restrictive the central bank really is.

library.title: Results versus expectations, and guidance
library.text: A company can beat estimates and still fall if the outlook disappoints: prices follow the future, not last quarter.

library.title: Short term: headlines. Long term: profits
library.text: Over days, prices move on fear and news. Over years, they follow earnings.

library.title: Read the curve, not only the level
library.text: If the 2-year moves most, the market is changing its view on the central bank. If the 30-year moves most, it is about inflation, growth or fiscal risk.

blocks.title: Stocks
blocks.headline: US stocks fell
blocks.what: S&P 500 -0.3% to 7,593, Nasdaq -0.4%, Dow -0.4%. On the week the S&P 500 is +3.2%.
why: Stocks weigh two things: company profits (the cash flows) and interest rates (the discount rate that turns future profits into today's price).
US payrolls came in at 165k against 65k expected: good for profits, bad for rates. Today the rate side won: stocks fell as investors priced a tougher Fed.
And it was broad: the average stock (-0.9%) beat the index (-0.3%).
Sectors: best Energy +1.5%, Utilities flat; worst Communication services -1.0%, Materials -1.3%.
Asia: KOSPI +2.6%. Asia trades first, so its session reflects the US session before it: on Wednesday the Nasdaq moved +1.6%. Korea and Japan are full of chip makers, so an AI sell-off hits them hard.
affects: Lords of Finance: the S&P 500 call depends on whether profits or rates win the tug of war this week.
Volatility: big index swings feed the VIX; calm days bring it down.
blocks.retain: Short term, stocks move on headlines and rates. Long term, they follow profits. Good economic news helps profits but can hurt through higher rates: which side wins depends on inflation.
blocks.ask: Why can the S&P 500 rise on a day when the average stock falls?

blocks.title: Interest rates & bonds
blocks.headline: US yields rose: 10-year 5.14%, 2-year 4.88%
blocks.what: US 10Y 5.14% (+13 bp today, +30 bp on the week); 2Y 4.88% (+16 bp).
why: US payrolls came in at 165k against 65k expected. Numbers that strong tell the Fed the economy can take higher rates, and they can keep inflation sticky, so a rate cut gets less likely and a hike more likely.
Traders now price a 100% chance of a hike on 9 December.

The 2-year (+16 bp) moved more than the 10-year (+13 bp). The 2-year follows what the Fed will do over the next two years; the 10-year mixes in long-term growth, inflation and government borrowing. So this was mainly a 'what will the Fed do' move.
In Europe, France pays 151 bp more than Germany to borrow for 10 years. That gap is the market's price for French debt risk.
affects: Dollar: higher US yields usually pull money into dollars (dollar index +0.3% today).
Growth stocks: most of their profits are far in the future, so higher rates hurt them most, like long bonds.
Gold: it pays no interest, so it loses appeal when yields rise.
Borrowers: mortgages and company loans are priced off these yields.
blocks.retain: The 2-year listens to the Fed. The 10-year listens to growth, inflation and how much the government borrows.
blocks.ask: If the 2-year rises more than the 10-year, what is the market telling you about the Fed?

blocks.title: Oil, gas & gold
blocks.headline: Oil +3.3%; gold -2.8%
blocks.what: Brent 95.83 (+3.3% today, -2.5% on the week); gold 3,878 (-2.8%).
why: Oil is set by supply and demand, plus geopolitics (Middle East, OPEC, Russia).
Our sources link it to: “Oil traders give peace a chance (but should they?)” (FT) / “Saudi oil production rebounds close to prewar levels” (FT).
European gas 94.81, +4.9% on the week: Europe's gas price swings with weather, storage levels and LNG shipments.
Gold fell as the dollar (+0.3%) and US yields (+13 bp) rose. Gold pays no interest, so higher yields make it less attractive, and a stronger dollar makes it dearer for buyers outside the US.
affects: Cheaper oil lowers inflation expectations, which eases pressure on the Fed; dearer oil does the opposite.
Airlines and transport gain from cheap fuel; energy producers lose (Energy sector +1.5% today).
Oil exporters' currencies (Canada, Norway) and oil-importing emerging markets feel it too.
Gold up usually means fear or falling real interest rates; gold down means calm or rising real rates.
blocks.retain: Oil is about supply, demand and geopolitics. Gold is about real interest rates, the dollar and fear.
blocks.ask: Oil fell 2.5% this week. Who wins and who loses?

blocks.title: Currencies
blocks.headline: Dollar firmer; EUR/USD 1.1055
blocks.what: Dollar index 103.18 (+0.3%); EUR/USD 1.1055 (-1.5% on the week); USD/JPY 159.85.
why: US 2-year yields moved +16 bp against flat for Germany. Money tends to flow to where it earns more, so a wider US advantage usually supports the dollar, and the dollar index did rise (+0.3%).
EUR/USD 1.1055: the euro is -5.9% this year. A Fed that may still hike, against an ECB on hold, keeps the dollar supported.
USD/JPY 159.85: the wide gap between US and Japanese interest rates keeps the yen weak. Japan's finance ministry has stepped in before when it fell near 160 per dollar, so traders watch that level.
affects: A stronger dollar weighs on gold and on commodities priced in dollars.
Emerging markets that borrow in dollars get squeezed when the dollar rises.
A weaker euro helps European exporters (cars, luxury, machinery) sell abroad.
blocks.retain: Currencies follow interest-rate gaps (money goes where it earns more) and risk appetite (in fear, money runs to the dollar, yen and Swiss franc).
blocks.ask: If the Fed hikes in December and the ECB stays on hold, what should happen to EUR/USD, and why?

blocks.title: Crypto
blocks.headline: Bitcoin -3.8% to 71,571
blocks.what: Bitcoin 71,571 (-3.8% today, -6.0% on the week, -18.4% this year).
why: Bitcoin usually trades like a high-risk tech stock: it does well when money is cheap and investors want risk.
Today it moved -3.8% while the Nasdaq moved -0.4%, so the move was crypto-specific rather than general risk appetite.
affects: Crypto-linked stocks (Coinbase, miners) move with it.
A falling bitcoin while tech rises is a warning sign about speculative appetite.
blocks.retain: Bitcoin behaves like a high-beta tech asset: it needs cheap money and appetite for risk.
blocks.ask: Bitcoin fell while the Nasdaq rose. What does that tell you about where risk appetite is going?

blocks.title: Fear gauges
blocks.headline: VIX 18.69 (+6.9%)
blocks.what: VIX 18.69 (+6.9% today, -33.7% on the week); MOVE 92.43.
why: The VIX measures how big investors expect S&P 500 swings to be over the next 30 days. Below 15 is calm, 15 to 20 normal, 20 to 30 stressed, above 30 panic. It is at 18.69.
It jumped 6.9% today after a calmer week (-33.7%).
The MOVE index (92.43, +7.5%) is the same idea for US Treasury yields.
affects: High fear pushes money into Treasuries, gold, the yen and the Swiss franc.
Options (insurance) get pricier, and funds that target a set risk level sell stocks.
blocks.retain: VIX is the fear gauge for stocks, MOVE for bonds. Fear spikes fast and fades slowly.
blocks.ask: Stocks rose today, but the VIX is still above 20. What does that tell you about how investors feel?

links.because: Money today becomes worth more than money tomorrow, so anything that pays far in the future (growth stocks, long bonds) is worth less now.

effects: Central bank likely hikes or delays cuts
links.because: Central banks fight inflation with higher rates, and markets price that before it happens.
With inflation calm, good news is good news. With inflation above target, good news can be bad news for stocks.
Oil feeds into transport, plastics and electricity: one company's revenue is another's cost.
Everything priced in dollars gets dearer for the rest of the world, and dollar debts get heavier.

effects: Treasuries, gold, yen and Swiss franc rise
links.because: In a scare, investors sell what is risky and buy what is safe: a flight to quality.

effects: Country spreads widen (e.g. France vs Germany)
links.because: More bonds to sell means buyers demand a higher return, and lenders charge more for perceived risk.

effects: Chip stocks and the Nasdaq swing most
links.because: A handful of tech giants are close to half of the S&P 500 'pizza', and chip makers dominate Asian indices.

lede.headline: US payrolls 165k vs 65k expected; December hike odds 100%; Bitcoin -3.8%
lede.standfirst: Stocks fell, S&P 500 -0.3% and Nasdaq -0.4%, with the 10Y +13 bp. Elsewhere, European gas rose 9.4% to 94.81.

sentences: Your markets briefing for the close of Thursday 12 November.
US payrolls came in far above expectations at 165 thousand against 65 thousand, with average hourly earnings 3.1 percent year on year against 2.9 percent.
That keeps a December hike in play, now priced at 100 percent.
Stocks fell, S and P 500 down 0.3 percent and Nasdaq down 0.4 percent, with the 10-year up 13 basis points.
Elsewhere, European gas rose 9.4 percent to 94.81.
Also: Brent oil up 3.3 percent, gold down 2.8 percent, bitcoin down 3.8 percent.
